beats.beat: Specialty chemicals is a description, not a product. The company's four lines — Functional Additives, Chemically Modified Minerals, Soft Minerals, Hard Minerals — are inputs sold to other manufacturers, which is why the filing lists 'diversified user industries' as one of its stated strengths rather than naming a single end market.

The dependence is acknowledged from both directions: the company says it derives synergies from 20 Microns Limited and lists 'support of our holding company' among its strengths, while also describing the marketing tie-up as a long-term arrangement with that same Corporate Promoter.
Customer concentration is disclosed and it is high. The top ten customers accounted for about 59% of revenue from operations in FY2017, 57% in FY2016 and 59% in FY2015.
Exports are small and narrow. Over the five years before the filing the company exported ₹1,068.18 lakh (about ₹10.68 crore) in total, to three countries: Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Sri Lanka.

The footprint is a set of named addresses rather than a plant count. The filing refers to manufacturing facilities at Plot 347, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat and at Plot 104/3, Thenkasi Road, Pathur Village, Alangulam, Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, and to a third site at Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia; administrative offices are in Bhuj and Udaipur. The proposed new plant at Plot 336 is a fourth address, not yet built.

The filing's own list of strengths is worth reading as a set because it tells you what the company thinks it competes on: a diversified product range, customers spread across industries, import substitution, backing from its holding company, product innovation and R&D, and its management team. Only the first three are argued with specifics elsewhere in the document.

beats.beat: The restated statements cover six periods, not five: the six months ended 30 September 2017, and the years ended 31 March 2017, 2016, 2015, 2014 and 2013. Everything below is in the filing's own unit, rupees lakh, and converted to crore at 100 lakh to a crore.

Profitability turned in the middle of the period. The company lost ₹0.27 crore in FY2013 and ₹0.12 crore in FY2014, then made ₹1.50 crore in FY2015. It fell to ₹0.90 crore in FY2016, recovered to ₹1.75 crore in FY2017, and reported ₹1.33 crore for the six months to 30 September 2017.
The pattern is not a straight line, and one year breaks it. FY2015's ₹1.50 crore profit was larger than FY2016's ₹0.90 crore, before FY2017 rose to ₹1.75 crore.

Earnings per share tracks the same path: negative ₹0.45 in FY2013 and ₹0.20 in FY2014, then positive at ₹2.47, ₹1.46 and ₹2.43 for FY2015, FY2016 and FY2017, and ₹1.48 for the six months to September 2017.

Cash generation is where the accounts get uncomfortable. Operating activities brought in ₹2.01 crore in FY2013, ₹1.28 crore in FY2014, ₹4.22 crore in FY2015 and ₹8.03 crore in FY2016 — then turned to an outflow of ₹3.50 crore in FY2017, before recovering to an inflow of ₹1.25 crore in the six months to September 2017.

That FY2017 swing is the number behind the company's own risk disclosure that it had negative cash flows in previous financial years and that sustained negative cash flow could affect growth and the business.

The balance sheet expanded over the same stretch, from ₹30.19 crore of total assets at 31 March 2013 to ₹32.74 crore at 31 March 2017 and ₹34.25 crore at 30 September 2017, having dipped to ₹25.93 crore at 31 March 2015.

What the accounts do not show in this excerpt: revenue or total income for any period, EBITDA, and the quantum of borrowings. The filing elsewhere refers to loan agreements with restrictive covenants and to unsecured loans that can be recalled at any time, so debt exists — but its size is not on the pages available here and must not be inferred.

beats.beat: Four promoters are named: Mr. Chandresh S. Parikh, Mr. Atil C. Parikh and Mr. Rajesh C. Parikh as individuals, and 20 Microns Limited as the corporate promoter, which is also the company's holding company and its sales channel.

The register is almost closed. Promoters hold 89,48,270 equity shares, or 99.76% of the pre-issue paid-up capital. The promoter group excluding the promoters holds another 21,510 shares, or 0.24%. Between them that is effectively 100%.

The capital base the issue dilutes: authorised share capital of ₹2,000.00 lakh, being 2,00,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, against issued, subscribed and paid-up capital of ₹897.00 lakh, being 89,70,000 shares of ₹10 each, as at 30 September 2017.

Related-party dealing is not a one-off. The filing states that related-party transactions exist for each of the last five financial years and for the six months to 30 September 2017, disclosed under Accounting Standard 18 — and the marketing of the company's products through the promoter's network sits on top of that.

The compliance record has admitted gaps. There have been instances of non-filing, incorrect filing or delayed filing of statutory forms with the Registrar of Companies, in some cases regularised later with additional fees.

More seriously, the company states it has not yet obtained certain statutory and regulatory licences, registrations and approvals required to operate its manufacturing facility at Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, and cannot assure it will not be penalised for that non-compliance.

Three smaller flags appear in the same section: the premises at Plot 347 GIDC Waghodia and Plot 104/3, Thenkasi Road, Pathur Village, Alangulam, Tirunelveli, plus the administrative offices in Bhuj and Udaipur, are not owned by the company; the corporate logo has not been registered; and the company, its promoters, its group company and its directors are parties to legal proceedings.
Contingent liabilities and commitments not provided for, as restated, were ₹29.11 lakh as at 30 September 2017.

beats.beat: Specialty chemicals sit inside the wider Indian chemicals industry but are counted separately because they are sold on performance, not on volume. The filing puts India's chemicals industry excluding pharmaceuticals and fertilisers at ₹5,800–6,200 billion in fiscal 2017, with specialty chemicals — other than agrochemicals and dyestuff — at roughly 17% of that, about ₹1,000 billion.

A second sizing figure appears in the same document: ₹1,443 billion for the specialty chemicals market, cited in the outlook section. The two numbers come from different places in the filing and measure different things; the writer should attribute each to its page rather than reconcile them.
Growth: the segment grew at 10-12% CAGR between fiscals 2014 and 2017, and CRISIL Research forecasts 12-14% CAGR going forward.

Which sub-segments are forecast to grow fastest matters for a company that will not break out its own revenue split. The filing lists construction chemicals at 15% CAGR over three years, water chemicals and personal care ingredients at 15% over five and three years respectively, surfactants at 13%, and textile chemicals and flavours and fragrances at 12%.
Two downstream markets are sized because they are the company's customers. Paints is a ₹401 billion market as of fiscal 2017, and the organised cosmetics and toiletries market is ₹430–460 billion.

Demand drivers named in the filing: rising intensity of consumption, end-use demand from a middle class the filing projects at 148 million households by 2030, improved consumption standards, and government policy including a Draft National Chemical Policy and permission for up to 100% foreign direct investment in the sector.

One global factor is spelled out: China dominates commodity chemicals and has paid less attention to specialties, and stricter environmental regulations introduced there in 2015 have curtailed its chemical output — a supply gap Indian producers can fill.

Structure and competition. The industry is fragmented, with small and medium enterprises holding 70-75% of the market, and the filing concedes that only a few Indian players have the scale or capability to compete with global majors on product development. No competitor is named anywhere in the excerpt.

Headwinds the filing acknowledges. India's chemicals trade has run a deficit every year from 2012-13 to 2016-17, with imports growing at 6.4% CAGR against exports at 6%. Exports into Europe must comply with REACH, the EU's registration and authorisation regime for chemicals.

Two policy changes frame the period the accounts cover: GST came into force on 1 July 2017, and four Petroleum, Chemicals and Petrochemicals Investment Regions have been approved in Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha with about ₹9 trillion of proposed investment.

industry.heading: The market it sells into
industry.purpose: Give the reader the size, the growth rate and the structure of Indian specialty chemicals, then the headwinds the filing itself names.

beats.beat: 20 Microns Nano Minerals is a specialty chemicals processor: it takes minerals and modifies them chemically into additives that other manufacturers put into their own products. It is part of the 20 Microns Limited group, which is both its promoter and its route to market.

The product list is four families, and the filing names them: Functional Additives, Chemically Modified Minerals, Soft Minerals and Hard Minerals. Functional Additives and Chemically Modified Minerals are described as the specialties; the soft and hard minerals are the mineral processing side.
It does not carry its own salesforce. The company markets and sells through a long-term arrangement with its Corporate Promoter, 20 Microns Limited, using that company's distribution network.
How a sale actually happens: customers place purchase orders. The filing states the company has no long-term or definitive agreements with customers, so volume and price are set order by order.

Ownership today is almost entirely inside the promoter family: 89,48,270 equity shares, or 99.76% of the pre-issue paid-up capital, sit with the promoters. A public listing will be the first time outsiders hold a stake.

The money from the issue has a named destination: capital expenditure for a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat, with the balance going to general corporate purposes. The shares are to be listed on the SME platform of NSE, NSE EMERGE.

intro.purpose: Orient a newcomer: what this company makes, how it reaches buyers, who owns it now, and what the listing is for.

beats.beat: The proceeds have two named uses. The first is capital expenditure to set up a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat — a fourth site, in the same industrial estate as two existing ones. The second is general corporate purposes.

A third object is structural rather than financial: creating a public trading market for the equity shares by listing on the SME platform of NSE, NSE EMERGE, which the filing says is meant to improve visibility and brand.
The intermediaries named in the excerpt: Vivro Financial Services Private Limited as lead manager, and Link Intime India Private Limited as registrar.

What the excerpt does not carry: the split between a fresh issue of new shares and an offer for sale of existing shares, the name of any selling shareholder, the total issue size, the price band, and the amount allocated to each object. None of those should be estimated — they are absent from the pages available here.

beats.beat: Risk one: the order book can vanish between quarters. The company has no long-term or definitive agreements with customers and relies on purchase orders to set volume, pricing and other sales terms. The mirror-image risk sits on the supply side, where there are also no long-term agreements with raw material suppliers.

Risk two: a handful of buyers carry the revenue. The top ten customers made up about 59% of revenue from operations in FY2017 — and 59% in FY2015 and 57% in FY2016, so this is a structural feature, not a one-year spike. Lose two or three of those accounts and the top line moves.

Risk three: FY2017 cash flow went backwards. Operating activities swung from an ₹8.03 crore inflow in FY2016 to a ₹3.50 crore outflow in FY2017. The company flags negative cash flows in previous years as a risk and says sustained negative cash flow could affect growth and the business.

Risk four: one plant is running without all its approvals. The company has not obtained certain statutory and regulatory licences, registrations and approvals required to operate the Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia facility, and says it cannot assure it will not be penalised for the non-compliance. It separately admits past non-filings, incorrect filings and delays with the Registrar of Companies.

Risk five: the company is knitted into its promoter group. Products are marketed and sold through the Corporate Promoter's network, related-party transactions have occurred in every one of the last five financial years, and unsecured loans taken by the company, the promoters, group companies or associates can be recalled by the lenders at any time. Loan agreements also carry restrictive covenants that the filing says could influence the company's ability to expand.
